ceratosaurus:enwiki:11.title: Ceratosaurus (Function of the nasal horn and osteoderms)

facts.statement: The genus Ceratosaurus was described by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1884.
facts.quote: authority: Marsh, 1884

facts.statement: Ceratosaurus lived during the Late Jurassic period, approximately 155 million years ago, in North America and Europe.
facts.quote: lived during the Late Jurassic period (around 155 m.y.a) in North America and Europe

facts.statement: The type species was described based on a nearly complete skeleton found in Garden Park, Colorado, within the Morrison Formation.
facts.quote: based on a nearly complete skeleton discovered in Garden Park, Colorado, in rocks belonging to the Morrison Formation

facts.statement: Ceratosaurus featured a prominent ridge-like horn on the snout and a pair of horns above the eyes.
facts.quote: prominent, ridge-like horn on the midline of the snout, and a pair of horns over the eyes

facts.statement: The dinosaur possessed deep jaws supporting proportionally very long, blade-like teeth.
facts.quote: deep jaws that supported proportionally very long, blade-like teeth

facts.statement: Although its forelimbs were very short, they remained fully functional.
facts.quote: forelimbs were very short, but remained fully functional

facts.statement: The original specimen is estimated to be between 5.3 m and 5.69 m in length.
facts.quote: The original specimen is estimated to be 5.3 m or 5.69 m long

facts.statement: The holotype specimen was discovered and excavated by farmer Marshall Parker Felch in 1883 and 1884.
facts.quote: discovered and excavated by farmer Marshall Parker Felch in 1883 and 1884

facts.statement: The specimen was encased in hard sandstone, causing the skull and spine to become heavily distorted during fossilization.
facts.quote: The specimen was found encased in hard sandstone, leading to the skull and spine being heavily distorted during fossilization

facts.statement: Charles Gilmore published an extensive redescription of the specimen in 1920.
facts.quote: In 1920, Charles Gilmore published an extensive redescription of this and the other theropod specimens received from New Haven

facts.statement: It is debated whether the nasal horn was a weapon or used solely for display, with recent studies suggesting it was for display.
facts.quote: The nasal horn was probably not used as a weapon as was originally suggested by Marsh, but more likely was used solely for display

facts.statement: While some paleontologists suggested Ceratosaurus hunted aquatic prey like fish, this hypothesis has been rejected by more recent studies.
facts.quote: while some paleontologists suggested that it hunted aquatic prey such as fish, this has been rejected by more recent studies

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that Ceratosaurus and other large theropods like Torvosaurus and Allosaurus occupied different ecological niches to reduce competition.
facts.quote: it has been suggested that these theropods occupied different ecological niches to reduce competition

facts.statement: Ceratosaurus gives its name to the clade Ceratosauria, which diverged early from the lineage leading to modern birds.
facts.quote: Ceratosaurus gives its name to Ceratosauria, a clade of theropod dinosaurs that diverged early on from the evolutionary lineage leading to modern birds

facts.statement: In 2000, a partial specimen from the Lourinhã Formation of Portugal provided evidence that the genus existed outside of North America.
facts.quote: In 2000, a partial specimen was excavated and described from the Lourinhã Formation of Portugal, providing evidence for the presence of the genus outside of North America

facts.statement: A significant Ceratosaurus skeleton was discovered in the early 1960s by James Madsen and his team in the Cleveland-Lloyd Dinosaur Quarry in Utah.
facts.quote: After the discovery of the holotype of C. nasicornis, a significant Ceratosaurus find was not made until the early 1960s, when paleontologist James Madsen and his team unearthed a fragmentary, disarticulated skeleton including the skull (UMNH VP 5278) in the Cleveland-Lloyd Dinosaur Quarry in Utah.

facts.statement: An articulated Ceratosaurus specimen was discovered in 1976 by Thor Erikson near Fruita, Colorado.
facts.quote: A second, articulated specimen including the skull (MWC 1) was discovered in 1976 by Thor Erikson, the son of paleontologist Lance Erikson, near Fruita, Colorado.

facts.statement: A Ceratosaurus specimen was discovered in 1992 in the Agate Basin Quarry in Utah.
facts.quote: A further specimen (BYU 881-12893) was discovered in 1992 in the Agate Basin Quarry southeast of Moore, Utah.

facts.statement: A juvenile Ceratosaurus skeleton was discovered in 1996 near Bone Cabin Quarry in Wyoming.
facts.quote: In 1996, a Ceratosaurus skeleton belonging to a juvenile individual was discovered near Bone Cabin Quarry in Wyoming.

facts.statement: A private Ceratosaurus specimen was resold at an auction in July 2025 for $30,510,000.
facts.quote: During an auction at Sotheby's on July 16, 2025, the specimen was resold at a price of $30,510,000.

facts.statement: German expeditions uncovered dinosaur remains in the Tendaguru Formation of Tanzania between 1909 and 1913.
facts.quote: From 1909 to 1913, German expeditions of the Berlin Museum für Naturkunde uncovered a diverse dinosaur fauna from the Tendaguru Formation in German East Africa, in what is now Tanzania.

facts.statement: Werner Janensch named the species Ceratosaurus roechlingi in 1925 based on fragmentary remains from the Mw quarry in Tanzania.
facts.quote: In 1925, Janensch named a new species of Ceratosaurus, C. roechlingi, based on fragmentary remains from the quarry "Mw" encompassing a quadrate bone, a fibula, fragmentary caudal vertebrae, and other fragments.

facts.statement: A Ceratosaurus specimen consisting of leg bones and teeth was described from Portugal in 2000 and 2006.
facts.quote: In 2000 and 2006, paleontologists led by Octávio Mateus described a find from the Lourinhã Formation of central-west Portugal (ML 352) as a new specimen of Ceratosaurus, consisting of a right femur (thigh bone), a left tibia (shin bone), and several isolated teeth recovered from the cliffs of Valmitão beach, between the municipalities of Lourinhã and Torres Vedras.

facts.statement: Teeth from the Tacuarembó Formation in Uruguay were described as belonging to Ceratosaurus in 2008.
facts.quote: In 2008, Matías Soto and Daniel Perea described teeth from the Tacuarembó Formation in Uruguay, including a presumed premaxillary tooth crown.

facts.statement: Madsen and Welles described two new Ceratosaurus species, C. dentisulcatus and C. magnicornis, in a 2000 monograph.
facts.quote: Both the Fruita and Cleveland-Lloyd specimens were described by Madsen and Samuel Paul Welles in a 2000 monograph, with the Utah specimen being assigned to the new species C. dentisulcatus and the Colorado specimen being assigned to the new species C. magnicornis.

facts.statement: As of 2025, the species C. dentisulcatus and C. magnicornis are generally considered synonyms of C. nasicornis.
facts.quote: As of 2025, both species are generally considered as synonyms of C. nasicornis.

facts.statement: Brooks Britt and colleagues suggested in 2000 that C. nasicornis is a juvenile and the other species represent adults of the same species.
facts.quote: Brooks Britt and colleagues, in 2000, claimed that the C. nasicornis holotype was in fact a juvenile individual, with the two larger species representing the adult state of a single species.

facts.statement: Rauhut and Carrano and Sampson argued that differences between Ceratosaurus species represent age-related or individual variation.
facts.quote: Oliver Rauhut, in 2003, and Matthew Carrano and Scott Sampson, in 2008, considered the anatomical differences between these species to represent ontogenetic (age-related) or individual variation.

facts.statement: Some authors question whether any finds from the Tendaguru Formation belong to Ceratosaurus due to a lack of diagnostic features.
facts.quote: Other authors questioned the assignment of any of the Tendaguru finds to Ceratosaurus, noting that none of these specimens displays features diagnostic for that genus.

facts.statement: Rauhut designated C. roechlingi and L. (?) stechowi as doubtful names because they are undiagnostic at the genus level.
facts.quote: In 2011, Rauhut found both C. roechlingi and Labrosaurus (?) stechowi to be possible ceratosaurids, but found them to be undiagnostic at genus level and designated them as nomina dubia (doubtful names).

facts.statement: Malafaia and colleagues assigned a Portuguese specimen to Ceratosaurus aff. C. nasicornis in 2015, questioning the validity of C. dentisulcatus.
facts.quote: In 2015, Elisabete Malafaia and colleagues, who questioned the validity of C. dentisulcatus, assigned the specimen to Ceratosaurus aff. Ceratosaurus nasicornis.

facts.statement: Carrano and Sampson confirmed a Portuguese find belongs to Ceratosaurus but concluded specific species assignment is not possible.
facts.quote: A 2008 review by Carrano and Sampson confirmed the assignment to Ceratosaurus, but concluded that the assignment to any specific species is not possible at present.

facts.statement: Soto and Perea noted that assigning Uruguayan teeth to Ceratosaurus is infeasible due to scant remains and requires caution regarding European and African material.
facts.quote: The authors, however, stressed that an assignment to Ceratosaurus is infeasible because the remains are scant and note that the assignment of the European and African material to Ceratosaurus has to be viewed with caution.

facts.statement: The species name dentisulcatus refers to parallel grooves on the inner sides of certain teeth.
facts.quote: The name dentisulcatus refers to the parallel grooves present on the inner sides of the premaxillary teeth and the first three teeth of the lower jaw in that specimen.

facts.statement: The species name magnicornis refers to a larger nasal horn.
facts.quote: Magnicornis points to the larger nasal horn.

facts.statement: A discovered Ceratosaurus skull was found disarticulated and strongly flattened sideways.
facts.quote: The skull, although reasonably complete, was found disarticulated and is strongly flattened sideways.

facts.statement: A discovered Ceratosaurus specimen was large but had not reached adult size, indicated by unfused skull sutures.
facts.quote: Although it was a large individual, it had not yet reached adult size, as indicated by unfused sutures between the skull bones.

facts.statement: A juvenile Ceratosaurus specimen is 34% smaller than the holotype and includes a complete skull and pelvis.
facts.quote: This specimen is 34% smaller than the C. nasicornis holotype and consists of a complete skull as well as 30% of the remainder of the skeleton including a complete pelvis.

facts.statement: Portuguese Ceratosaurus bones were found in sandstones thought to be late Kimmeridgian in age.
facts.quote: The bones were found embedded in yellow to brown, fine-grained sandstones, which were deposited by rivers as floodplain deposits and belong to the lower levels of the Porto Novo Member, which is thought to be late Kimmeridgian in age.

facts.statement: The Cleveland-Lloyd specimen represents one of the largest-known Ceratosaurus specimens.
facts.quote: This find represents one of the largest-known Ceratosaurus specimens.

facts.statement: A Ceratosaurus skeleton was bought by a private museum and has not been scientifically described.
facts.quote: The specimen was bought by the North American Museum of Ancient Life, but because this museum is private rather than a public repository, the specimen has not been scientifically described.

facts.statement: Werner Janensch assigned three dorsal vertebrae from a juvenile to Ceratosaurus in 1920.
facts.quote: In 1920, German paleontologist Werner Janensch assigned three dorsal vertebrae of a juvenile individual from the quarry "TL" to Ceratosaurus, as Ceratosaurus sp. (of uncertain species).

facts.statement: Fragmentary Ceratosaurus remains have been found in various localities within the Morrison Formation.
facts.quote: Besides these five skeletal finds, fragmentary Ceratosaurus remains have been reported from various localities from stratigraphic zones 2 and 4-6 of the Morrison Formation, including some of the major fossil sites of the formation.

facts.statement: Marsh used the name Labrosaurus sulcatus in 1896 for a single tooth figure.
facts.quote: In 1896, Marsh used the name Labrosaurus sulcatus in a caption for a figure depicting a single tooth (YPM 1936).

facts.statement: Studies identified a tooth originally named Labrosaurus sulcatus as belonging to Ceratosaurus.
facts.quote: Subsequent studies identified the tooth as belonging to Ceratosaurus, either from the front portion of the lower jaw or the premaxilla of the upper jaw.

facts.statement: A single Ceratosaurus tooth was found in Moutier, Switzerland.
facts.quote: Other reports include a single tooth found in Moutier, Switzerland.

facts.statement: Rowe and Gauthier mentioned a potential Ceratosaurus species based on 25 large teeth from Tendaguru in 1990.
facts.quote: In 1990, Timothy Rowe and Jacques Gauthier mentioned yet another Ceratosaurus species from Tendaguru, Ceratosaurus ingens, which purportedly was erected by Janensch in 1920 and was based on 25 isolated, very large teeth up to 15 cm in length.

facts.statement: Janensch assigned the species C. ingens to Megalosaurus, suggesting the name might be a copying error.
facts.quote: However, Janensch assigned this species to Megalosaurus, not to Ceratosaurus. Therefore, this name might be a simple copying error.

facts.statement: Rauhut suggested in 2011 that Megalosaurus ingens might be a carcharodontosaurid rather than related to Ceratosaurus.
facts.quote: Rauhut, in 2011, showed that Megalosaurus ingens was not closely related to either Megalosaurus or Ceratosaurus, but possibly represents a carcharodontosaurid instead.

facts.statement: Malafaia and colleagues assigned a Portuguese specimen to Ceratosaurus aff. C. nasicornis in 2015.
facts.quote: In 2015, Elisabete Malafaia and colleagues, who questioned the validity of C. dentisulcatus, assigned the specimen to Ceratosaurus aff. Ceratosaurus nasicornis.

facts.statement: Additional bones of a Portuguese Ceratosaurus specimen were exposed due to cliff erosion.
facts.quote: Additional bones of this individual (SHN (JJS)-65), including a left femur, a right tibia, and a partial left fibula (calf bone), were since exposed due to progressing cliff erosion.

facts.statement: Additional Portuguese Ceratosaurus bones were donated to a natural history society and described in 2015.
facts.quote: Although initially part of a private collection, these additional elements became officially curated after the private collection was donated to the Sociedade de História Natural in Torres Vedras and were described in detail in 2015.

facts.statement: Soto and Perea described Uruguayan teeth as Ceratosaurus in 2008.
facts.quote: In 2008, Matías Soto and Daniel Perea described teeth from the Tacuarembó Formation in Uruguay, including a presumed premaxillary tooth crown.

facts.statement: The combination of features on Uruguayan teeth is only known from Ceratosaurus.
facts.quote: These features are, in this combination, only known from Ceratosaurus.

facts.statement: Soto and colleagues described additional Uruguayan Ceratosaurus teeth in 2020.
facts.quote: In 2020, Soto and colleagues described additional Ceratosaurus teeth from the same formation that further support their earlier interpretation.

facts.statement: The genus Ceratosaurus is known from teeth found in Mygatt Moore Quarry, Colorado.
facts.quote: In Mygatt Moore Quarry, Colorado, the genus is known from teeth.

facts.statement: A large shoulder blade was reported from Como Bluff in Wyoming.
facts.quote: A large shoulder blade (scapulocoracoid) was reported from Como Bluff in Wyoming.

facts.statement: A specimen from the Dry Mesa Quarry in Colorado includes a shoulder blade and bone fragments.
facts.quote: Another specimen stems from the Dry Mesa Quarry of Colorado and includes a left scapulocoracoid, as well as fragments of vertebrae and limb bones.

facts.statement: An isolated premaxilla was found at Dinosaur National Monument in Utah.
facts.quote: Dinosaur National Monument, Utah, yielded an isolated right premaxilla (DNM 972).

facts.statement: Longitudinal grooves on a tooth led to the assignment of similar teeth from Tanzania and Switzerland to Labrosaurus.
facts.quote: The tooth has characteristic longitudinal grooves, which resulted in the assignment of several other, similar teeth from Tanzania and Switzerland to Labrosaurus.

facts.statement: A Swiss tooth was transferred to Labrosaurus by Janensch in 1920, originally included in Megalosaurus by Greppin in 1870.
facts.quote: The tooth was originally included in Megalosaurus meriani by Jean-Baptiste Greppin in 1870, but transferred to the genus Labrosaurus, as Labrosaurus (?) stechowi, by Janensch in 1920.

facts.statement: A Swiss tooth was assigned to Ceratosaurus by Madsen and Welles in 2000 and to Ceratosauria by Carrano in 2012.
facts.quote: The tooth was assigned to Ceratosaurus sp. (of unknown species) by Madsen and Welles in their 2000 study, and to an indeterminate member of Ceratosauria by Carrano and colleagues in 2012.

facts.statement: Ceratosaurus was a bipedal dinosaur that moved on powerful legs with reduced arms.
facts.quote: As a biped, it moved on powerful legs, while its arms were reduced in size.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen USNM 4735 of Ceratosaurus nasicornis was estimated to be 5.3 m or 5.69 m long.
facts.quote: Specimen USNM 4735, the first discovered skeleton and holotype of Ceratosaurus nasicornis, was an individual 5.3 m or 5.69 m long according to separate sources.

facts.statement: Recent accounts revise the weight of the holotype specimen to 418 kg, 524 kg, or 670 kg.
facts.quote: In more recent accounts, this was revised to 418 kg, 524 kg, or 670 kg.

facts.statement: Foster estimated in 2020 that specimen MWC 1 was slightly larger than the holotype, weighing 438 kg.
facts.quote: The second skeleton, MWC 1, was estimated to be slightly larger than the holotype specimen by Foster in 2020, at 438 kg.

facts.statement: Specimen BYU 881-12893 was estimated at 1120 kg by Sombathy and colleagues.
facts.quote: The third specimen, BYU 881-12893, was estimated at 1120 kg by Sombathy and colleagues.

facts.statement: Specimen ML 352, discovered in Portugal in 2000, was estimated to be 6 m long and weigh 600 kg.
facts.quote: Another specimen, ML 352, discovered in Portugal in 2000, was estimated at 6 m in length and 600 kg in weight.

facts.statement: The skull length of the largest Ceratosaurus specimen is estimated at 79 cm.
facts.quote: The skull length of the largest specimen is estimated at 79 cm in length.

facts.statement: The most distinctive feature of Ceratosaurus was a prominent horn on the skull midline behind the nostrils, formed from fused nasal bones.
facts.quote: The most distinctive feature was a prominent horn situated on the skull midline behind the bony nostrils, which was formed from fused protuberances of the left and right nasal bones.

facts.statement: In life, the bony horn core would have supported a keratinous sheath.
facts.quote: In the living animal, this core would have supported a keratinous sheath.

facts.statement: In life, the horn was likely more elongated due to the keratinous sheath.
facts.quote: In the living animal, the horn would likely have been more elongated due to its keratinous sheath.

facts.statement: The premaxillary bones at the tip of the snout contained only three teeth on each side, fewer than in most other theropods.
facts.quote: The premaxillary bones, which formed the tip of the snout, contained merely three teeth on each side, less than in most other theropods.

facts.statement: In the holotype, the upper jaw teeth are 7 cm long, surpassing the minimum height of the lower jaw.
facts.quote: In the holotype, they are 7 cm in length, which even surpasses the minimum height of the lower jaw.

facts.statement: The Ceratosaurus tail consisted of approximately 50 vertebrae and made up about half of the animal's total length.
facts.quote: The tail comprised around 50 caudal vertebrae and was about half of the animal's total length.

facts.statement: The tail of the Ceratosaurus holotype was estimated to be 9.33 feet long.
facts.quote: In the holotype, it was estimated at 9.33 ft.

facts.statement: In Ceratosaurus, the shoulder blade was fused with the coracoid to form a single bone with no visible separation between the two parts.
facts.quote: The scapula (shoulder blade) was fused with the coracoid, forming a single bone without any visible demarcation between the two original elements.

facts.statement: Unlike most advanced theropods that had three fingers, Ceratosaurus retained four digits on its hands, with the fourth digit being smaller.
facts.quote: In contrast to most more-derived theropods, which showed only three digits on each hand (digits I–III), Ceratosaurus retained four digits, with digit IV being reduced in size.

facts.statement: The foot of Ceratosaurus had three weight-bearing digits, numbered II, III, and IV.
facts.quote: The pes (foot) consisted of three weight-bearing digits, numbered II–IV.

facts.statement: Ceratosaurus uniquely among theropods had small, elongated, and irregular skin bones called osteoderms running along the midline of its body.
facts.quote: Uniquely among theropods, Ceratosaurus possessed small, elongated, and irregularly formed osteoderms (skin bones) along the midline of its body.

facts.statement: Osteoderms in Ceratosaurus were found on neck vertebrae 4 and 5 and tail vertebrae 4 to 10, likely forming a continuous row from the skull base to the tail.
facts.quote: Such osteoderms have been found above the neural spines of cervical vertebrae 4 and 5, as well as caudal vertebrae 4 to 10, and probably formed a continuous row that might have extended from the base of the skull to most of the tail.

facts.statement: Besides the midline row, Ceratosaurus had other skin bones, including a 58 mm by 70 mm quadrangular plate found with the holotype.
facts.quote: Apart from the body midline, the skin contained additional osteoderms, as indicated by a 58 mm by 70 mm large, roughly quadrangular plate found together with the holotype.

facts.statement: Some researchers suggest that Ceratosaurus lost its wrist bones because none have been found in any specimen.
facts.quote: Carpal bones were not known from any specimen, leading some authors to suggest that they were lost in the genus.

facts.statement: A 2016 study by Matthew Carrano and Jonah Choiniere suggests that Ceratosaurus likely had cartilaginous wrist bones, based on gaps and textures seen in fossil casts.
facts.quote: In a 2016 paper, Matthew Carrano and Jonah Choiniere suggested that one or more cartilaginous (not bony) carpals were probably present, as indicated by a gap present between the forearm bones and the metacarpals, as well as by the surface texture within this gap seen in the cast.

facts.statement: While Othniel Marsh thought Ceratosaurus lost its first toe in 1884, Charles Gilmore showed in 1920 that an attachment site on the foot proved this toe was present.
facts.quote: Marsh, in his original 1884 description, assumed that this digit was lost in Ceratosaurus, but Charles Gilmore, in his 1920 monograph, noted an attachment area on the second metatarsal demonstrating the presence of this digit.

facts.statement: Marsh originally classified Ceratosaurus as the sole member of the new family Ceratosauridae and the new infraorder Ceratosauria.
facts.quote: Marsh made Ceratosaurus the only member of both a new family, Ceratosauridae, and a new infraorder, Ceratosauria.

facts.statement: Marsh's original claim that Ceratosauria was a distinct group gained acceptance only after cladistic analysis was established in the 1980s.
facts.quote: It was not until the establishment of cladistic analysis in the 1980s, however, that Marsh's original claim of Ceratosauria as a distinct group gained ground.

facts.statement: Oliver Rauhut proposed in 2004 that Genyodectes is the sister taxon of Ceratosaurus due to both having exceptionally long upper teeth.
facts.quote: Oliver Rauhut, in 2004, proposed Genyodectes as the sister taxon of Ceratosaurus, as both genera are characterized by exceptionally long teeth in the upper jaw.

facts.statement: Wang and colleagues concluded in 2017 that Noasauridae are more basal than Ceratosaurus and not nested within Abelisauroidea.
facts.quote: Shuo Wang and colleagues, in 2017, concluded that Noasauridae were not nested within Abelisauroidea as was previously assumed, but instead were more basal than Ceratosaurus.

facts.statement: Wang and colleagues found that Ceratosaurus and Genyodectes form a clade with the Argentinian genus Eoabelisaurus.
facts.quote: Wang and colleagues furthermore found that Ceratosaurus and Genyodectes form a clade with the Argentinian genus Eoabelisaurus.

facts.statement: Proceratosaurus is now considered a basal member of Tyrannosauroidea, a more derived clade of theropods.
facts.quote: Today, Proceratosaurus is considered a basal member of Tyrannosauroidea, a much more derived clade of theropod dinosaurs.

facts.statement: Donald Henderson suggested in 1998 that Ceratosaurus used its long teeth as fangs for quick, slashing bites with concentrated force due to its narrow skull.
facts.quote: In 1998, Donald Henderson compared the long-snouted skull of Ceratosaurus with that of a dog: The longer teeth would have been used as fangs to deliver quick, slashing bites, with the bite force concentrated at a smaller area due to the narrow skull.

facts.statement: Snively and Russell suggested in 2007 that Ceratosaurus could make powerful upward and sideways head movements.
facts.quote: In 2007, Eric Snively and Anthony Russell reconstructed the neck muscles of Ceratosaurus and suggested that upwards and sidewards movements of the head were powerful.

facts.statement: Snively and Russell concluded that Ceratosaurus was suited for quick slashing strikes similar to those of a Komodo dragon.
facts.quote: The short moment arms of most neck muscles suggest quick movements. Consequently, these authors likewise concluded that the skull was suited for quick slashing strikes, which they compared to those of the Komodo dragon.

facts.statement: Oswald and Curtice argued in 2026 that Ceratosaurus used its long teeth like sabre-tooth cats to quickly kill smaller prey such as Nanosaurus, Dryosaurus, Camptosaurus, and juvenile sauropods.
facts.quote: In 2026, Taylor Oswald and Brian Curtice argued that the very long teeth of Ceratosaurus had a function similar to those of sabre-tooth cats and were used to quickly kill prey of smaller size, possibly including Nanosaurus, Dryosaurus, Camptosaurus, and juvenile sauropods.

facts.statement: Holliday and Witmer concluded in 2008 that muscle-powered cranial kinesis was likely absent in most dinosaurs.
facts.quote: In a 2008 study, Casey Holliday and Lawrence Witmer re-evaluated similar claims made for other dinosaurs, concluding that the presence of muscle-powered cranial kinesis cannot be proven for any dinosaur species and was likely absent in most.

facts.statement: A pubic foot of an Allosaurus shows bite marks likely made by Ceratosaurus or Torvosaurus.
facts.quote: An Allosaurus pubic foot shows marks by the teeth of another theropod, probably Ceratosaurus or Torvosaurus.

facts.statement: The location and mass of the bitten Allosaurus bone indicate it was being scavenged.
facts.quote: The location of the bone in the body (along the bottom margin of the torso and partially shielded by the legs) and the fact that it was among the most massive in the skeleton indicates that the Allosaurus was being scavenged.

facts.statement: Bite marks on Allosaurus fossils suggest scavenging by other theropods or by another Allosaurus.
facts.quote: bite marks found on Allosaurus material suggest scavenging, either from the other theropods or from another Allosaurus.

facts.statement: Marsh and Gilmore considered the nasal horn of Ceratosaurus a powerful weapon for offense and defense.
facts.quote: In 1884, Marsh considered the nasal horn of Ceratosaurus to be a "most powerful weapon" for both offensive and defensive purposes and Gilmore, in 1920, concurred with this interpretation.

facts.statement: David Norman suggested in 1985 the horn was likely used for intraspecific combat among males rather than defense against predators.
facts.quote: In 1985, David Norman believed that the horn was "probably not for protection against other predators," but might instead have been used for intraspecific combat among male ceratosaurs contending for breeding rights.

facts.statement: Rowe and Gauthier suggested in 1990 the nasal horn was used solely for display and played no role in physical fights.
facts.quote: In 1990, Rowe and Gauthier went further, suggesting that the nasal horn of Ceratosaurus was "probably used for display purposes alone" and played no role in physical confrontations.

facts.statement: If the horn was used for display, it was likely brightly colored.
facts.quote: If used for display, the horn likely would have been brightly colored.

facts.statement: Ceratosaurus had strongly shortened metacarpals and phalanges, leading to debate over whether its hand retained a grasping function.
facts.quote: The strongly shortened metacarpals and phalanges of Ceratosaurus raise the question as to whether the hand retained the grasping function assumed for other basal theropods.

facts.statement: A 2016 study by Carrano and Jonah Choiniere suggested that despite its shortening, the Ceratosaurus hand fulfilled its original grasping function due to morphological similarities with other basal theropods.
facts.quote: In a 2016 paper on the anatomy of the Ceratosaurus hand, Carrano and Jonah Choiniere stressed the great morphological similarity of the hand with those of other basal theropods, suggesting that it still fulfilled its original grasping function, despite its shortening.

facts.statement: Ceratosaurus had well-preserved olfactory bulb impressions that were smaller than those in Tyrannosaurus, suggesting a less keen sense of smell than the latter.
facts.quote: The impressions for the olfactory bulbs, which house the sense of smell, are well-preserved. While similar to those of Allosaurus, they were smaller than in Tyrannosaurus, which is thought to have been equipped with a very keen sense of smell.

facts.statement: Ceratosaurus had an enlarged foremost semicircular canal, a feature generally found in bipedal animals.
facts.quote: The foremost of the semicircular canals was enlarged, a feature generally found in bipedal animals.

facts.statement: The orientation of the lateral semicircular canal in Ceratosaurus indicates that its head and neck were held horizontally in a neutral position.
facts.quote: The orientation of the lateral semicircular canal indicates that the head and neck were held horizontally in neutral position.

facts.statement: It is debated whether the fusion of metatarsals II to IV in the Ceratosaurus holotype was a natural feature or the result of a healed fracture, a controversy that began in 1890.
facts.quote: The presence of this feature in Ceratosaurus became controversial in 1890, when Georg Baur speculated that the fusion in the holotype was the result of a healed fracture.

facts.statement: A 1999 analysis by Darren Tanke and Bruce Rothschild suggested that the metatarsal fusion in Ceratosaurus was pathological, confirming earlier claims by Georg Baur.
facts.quote: A 1999 analysis by Darren Tanke and Bruce Rothschild suggested that the fusion was indeed pathological, confirming the earlier claim of Baur.

facts.statement: Pathological evidence in Ceratosaurus includes a stress fracture in a foot bone and a broken tooth showing signs of further wear after the break.
facts.quote: Other reports of pathologies include a stress fracture in a foot bone assigned to the genus, as well as a broken tooth of an unidentified species of Ceratosaurus that shows signs of further wear received after the break.

facts.statement: Changyu Yun observed that the conical frontmost teeth and fused nasal bones of Ceratosaurus possibly indicate that it relied more on fish than other theropods.
facts.quote: Yun observed that the frontmost teeth are conical and the nasal bones are fused together, possibly indicating that Ceratosaurus relied more on fish than other theropods.

facts.statement: Ceratosaurus lived during the Late Jurassic period, specifically within the Kimmeridgian and early Tithonian stages, between 156.3 and 146.8 million years ago.
facts.quote: According to radiometric dating, the age of the formation ranges between 156.3 million years old at its base and 146.8 million years old at the top, which places it in the late Oxfordian, Kimmeridgian, and early Tithonian stages of the Late Jurassic.

facts.statement: A partial specimen indicates that Ceratosaurus was also present in the Lourinhã Formation of Portugal.
facts.quote: A partial Ceratosaurus specimen indicates the presence of the genus in the Portuguese Porto Novo Member of the Lourinhã Formation.

facts.statement: The genus Ceratosaurus was named by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1884.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Marsh, 1884

facts.statement: The type species of the genus Ceratosaurus is Ceratosaurus nasicornis.
facts.quote: type_species: Ceratosaurus nasicornis

facts.statement: Ceratosaurus belongs to the superfamily Ceratosauria.
facts.quote: superfamilia: Ceratosauria

facts.statement: Ceratosaurus is classified within the family Ceratosauridae.
facts.quote: familia: Ceratosauridae

facts.statement: Ceratosaurus was a rare member of the theropod fauna, found at an average rate of 7.5 to 1 compared to Allosaurus in sites where both species coexist.
facts.quote: Ceratosaurus was a rare element of the theropod fauna, as it is outnumbered by Allosaurus at an average rate of 7.5 to 1 in sites where they co-occur.

facts.statement: A life-sized model of Ceratosaurus appeared in the 1914 film Brute Force, which is possibly the first live-action dinosaur film.
facts.quote: A life-sized model of Ceratosaurus threatens cave people in D. W. Griffith's 1914 silent movie Brute Force, possibly the first ever live-action dinosaur film.

facts.statement: Ceratosaurus was one of the first dinosaurs discovered and the fourth theropod to be found.
facts.quote: Ceratosaurus fue uno de los primeros dinosaurios descubiertos y el cuarto terópodo en descubrirse

facts.statement: Ceratosaurus lived during the late Jurassic Period, approximately 153 to 148 million years ago.
facts.quote: que vivió a finales del período Jurásico, hace aproximadamente 153 y 148 millones de años, en el Kimmeridgiense y el Titoniense

facts.statement: Fossils of Ceratosaurus have been found in what is now North America, Africa, Uruguay, and Europe.
facts.quote: en lo que hoy es Norteamérica, África, Uruguay y Europa

facts.statement: Ceratosaurus is the type member of the infraorder Ceratosauria, which is named after it.
facts.quote: por esto fue el miembro tipo del infraorden Ceratosauria el cual lleva su nombre

facts.statement: Ceratosaurus followed the typical body plan of large theropod dinosaurs, being bipedal with powerful hind legs and reduced arms.
facts.quote: Ceratosaurus siguió el plan corporal típico de los grandes dinosaurios terópodos. Fue bípedo y se movió sobre poderosas patas traseras, mientras que sus brazos se redujeron en tamaño

facts.statement: Ceratosaurus is characterized by a horn-like structure on the dorsal part of its skull, located behind the nasal openings.
facts.quote: Ceratosaurus se caracteriza por tener en su cráneo una estructura semejante a un cuerno en la parte dorsal de la cabeza, colocado atrás de las fosas nasales

facts.statement: Unlike most theropods, Ceratosaurus possessed dermal armor with small osteoderms located along its back.
facts.quote: Único entre la mayoría de los terópodos, Ceratosaurus poseía una armadura dérmica, con pequeños osteodermos que se situaban en medio de la espalda

facts.statement: The tail of Ceratosaurus measured about half the total body length and was thin and flexible with high vertebral spines along its back.
facts.quote: Su cola medía alrededor de la mitad de la longitud total del cuerpo, y era delgada y flexible, con altas espinas vertebrales, que se presentaban en el medio de su dorso

facts.statement: The holotype specimen of Ceratosaurus corresponds to an individual approximately 5.3 meters long and 2 meters high.
facts.quote: El espécimen holotipo de Ceratosaurus corresponde a un individuo de unos 5,3 metros de largo y 2 metros de alto

facts.statement: The largest known species, C. dentisulcatus, was informally estimated by Madsen to be around 8.8 meters long.
facts.quote: El más grande de estos, C. dentisuclatus, fue estimado informalmente por Madsen en alrededor de 8,8 metros de largo

facts.statement: Although it appeared like a typical theropod at first glance, Ceratosaurus had a very large skull relative to its body and a large nasal horn.
facts.quote: El Ceratosaurus, a primera vista parecía un terópodo bastante típico, sin embargo, su cráneo era bastante grande en proporción al resto de su cuerpo y poseía un cuerno nasal muy grande

facts.statement: The skull was quite large relative to the rest of the body, measuring 62.5 centimeters in length in the holotype.
facts.quote: El cráneo era bastante grande en proporción al resto de su cuerpo, midiendo 62.5 centímetros de longitud en el holotipo

facts.statement: Only the bony core of the horn is known from fossils; in a living animal, this core would have supported a keratinous sheath.
facts.quote: Solo el núcleo del cuerno óseo es conocido por los fósiles, en el animal viviente, este núcleo habría soportado una envoltura queratinosa

facts.statement: In the holotype, the core of the horn measures 13 centimeters long and 2 centimeters wide at its base.
facts.quote: En el holotipo, el núcleo del cuerno mide 13 centímetros de largo y 2 centímetros de ancho en su base

facts.statement: In addition to the large nasal horn, Ceratosaurus had smaller horn crests in front of each eye, similar to those of Allosaurus.
facts.quote: Además del cuerno nasal grande, Ceratosaurus poseía crestas de cuerno más pequeñas delante de cada ojo, similar a las de Allosaurus

facts.statement: The upper jaws were lined with 12 to 15 blade-like teeth on each side.
facts.quote: Las mandíbulas superiores estaban forradas con entre 12 y 15 dientes similares a cuchillas en cada lado

facts.statement: The premaxilla bone, forming the tip of the snout, contained only three teeth on each half, fewer than in most other theropods.
facts.quote: El hueso premaxilar, que formaba la punta del hocico, contenía solamente tres dientes en cada mitad, menos que en la mayoría de los demás terópodos

facts.statement: The dental crowns of the upper jaw were exceptionally long, measuring up to 9.3 centimeters in length in the largest sample.
facts.quote: Las coronas dentales de la mandíbula superior fueron excepcionalmente largas, midiendo hasta 9.3 centímetros de longitud en la muestra más grande

facts.statement: The arms of Ceratosaurus were relatively short, similar to other basal representatives of Ceratosauria.
facts.quote: Los brazos de Ceratosaurus eran relativamente cortos, al igual que en otros representantes basales de Ceratosauria

facts.statement: Ceratosaurus possessed four fingers on its hand, a very ancient characteristic in theropods.
facts.quote: Ceratosaurus poseía cuatro dedos en la mano, una característica muy antigua en los terópodos

facts.statement: The sacrum consisted of 6 fused sacral vertebrae.
facts.quote: El sacro consistió en 6 vértebras sacras fusionadas

facts.statement: Fifty vertebrae make up the tail.
facts.quote: 50 vértebras conforman la cola

facts.statement: Unlike most other theropods, Ceratosaurus had a row of small, elongated, irregularly shaped osteoderms running along the middle of its neck, back, and most of its tail.
facts.quote: A diferencia de la mayoría delos otros terópodos, Ceratosaurus poseía una fila de osteodermos pequeños, alargados y deforma irregular que corren por la mitad de su cuello, espalda y la mayor parte de su cola

facts.statement: Two species, Ceratosaurus roechlingi from Tanzania and Ceratosaurus meriani from Switzerland, are still considered dubious.
facts.quote: Dos especies, de las muchas que alguna vez se han nombrado, todavía son consideradas dudosas, Ceratosaurus roechlingi de Tanzania y Ceratosaurus meriani de Suiza

facts.statement: Fossils of Ceratosaurus have been found at the Cleveland-Lloyd Dinosaur Quarry in central Utah and the Mesa Seca Quarry in Colorado.
facts.quote: Los restos fósiles de Ceratosaurus han sido encontrados en la Mina del Dinosaurio de Cleveland Lloyd en Utah central y en la Mina de Mesa Seca en Colorado.

facts.statement: The type species, Ceratosaurus nasicornis, was described by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1884 and redescribed by Gilmore in 1920.
facts.quote: La especie tipo, descrita por Othniel Charles Marsh en 1884 y redescrita por Gilmore en 1920, es Ceratosaurus nasicornis.

facts.statement: Two new species, C. magnicornis and C. dentisulcatus, were described in 2000 by Madsen and Welles.
facts.quote: Dos nuevas especies distintas fueron descritas en el año 2000 por Madsen & Welles, son C. magnicornis y C. dentisulcatus.

facts.statement: The species C. magnicornis and C. dentisulcatus are currently considered synonyms of C. nasicornis.
facts.quote: Ambas basadas en ejemplares más grandes, aunque actualmente se las considera sinónimos de C. nasicornis.

facts.statement: Additional species such as C. roechlingi, C. ingens, C. stechowi, and C. meriani have been named from material found in Portugal and elsewhere.
facts.quote: Más especies adicionales han sido nombradas alrededor del mundo, incluyendo C. roechlingi, C. ingens, C. stechowi y C. meriani, en Portugal han sido descritas de material menos completo porlogeneral referido a C. nasicornis.

facts.statement: Ceratosaurus is present in stratigraphic zones 2 and 4.6 of the Morrison Formation.
facts.quote: Ceratosaurus está presente en las zonas estratigráficas 2 y 4.6 de la Formación Morrison.

facts.statement: The type species C. nasicornis was found in the Brushy Basin of the Morrison Formation in Colorado, USA.
facts.quote: C. nasicornis (Marsh, 1884) especie tipo, encontrado en la Cuenca Brushy de la Formación Morrison, Colorado, EE. UU..

facts.statement: The dubious species C. meriani was originally described by Greppin in 1870 from material found in Switzerland.
facts.quote: C. meriani (N.D.) (Greppin, 1870 (originalmente "Megalosaurus" meriani), encontrado en Suiza, Europa.

facts.statement: The dubious species C. roechlingi was described by Janensch in 1925 from the upper sauropod bed of the Tendaguru Formation in Tanzania.
facts.quote: "C." roechlingi (N.D.) (Janensch, 1925)>Ceratosauria incertae sedis, encontrado en Cama superior de Saurios de la Formación Tendaguru, Tanzania.

facts.statement: The name Ceratosaurus means "horned lizard" in Greek, derived from words for "horn" and "lizard".
facts.quote: El nombre Ceratosaurus que en griego significa "lagarto de cuerno" proviene de los términos κερας/κερατος, keras/keratos que significa "cuerno" y σαυρος/sauros "lagarto".

facts.statement: The name refers to the horn located above the nose.
facts.quote: Su nombre hace referencia al cuerno que tiene por encima de la nariz.

facts.statement: Ceratosaurus had a long, flexible body and a tail that resembled that of a crocodile.
facts.quote: Ceratosaurus tuvo un cuerpo largo y flexible, con una cola que recuerda a la de un cocodrilo.

facts.statement: Its crocodile-like tail suggests it may have been a good swimmer.
facts.quote: Esto sugiere que pudo haber sido un buen nadador.

facts.statement: Ceratosaurus fossils have been found at Garden Park in Colorado alongside Allosaurus remains.
facts.quote: Ceratosaurus, ha sido encontrado en el sitio arqueológico Garden Park en Colorado, junto a los restos de Allosaurus.

facts.statement: Fossils of Ceratosaurus, Allosaurus, and Torvosaurus have been found together at the Cleveland-Lloyd Quarry, Mesa Quarry, and Dinosaur National Monument.
facts.quote: También ha sido hallado en la Cantera The Cleveland-Lloyd en Utah, en la Mesa Cantera en Colorado y en el Monumento nacional Dinosaurio en la frontera de Colorado y Utah cada una tenía los restos de al menos tres terópodos: Ceratosaurus, Allosaurus y Torvosaurus.

facts.statement: Remains of Ceratosaurus and Allosaurus recovered in Wyoming indicate they lived together.
facts.quote: En Wyoming se recuperaron los restos de Ceratosaurus, y Allosaurus lo cual indica que vivieron juntos.

facts.statement: A 1998 study by Henderson noted that Ceratosaurus had a high, wide, short skull with curved teeth and a long snout with longer vertical lower teeth, contrasting with Allosaurus.
facts.quote: Henderson en 1998 examinó a un espécimen de Ceratosaurus y dos morfotipos de Allosaurus las cuales pertenecen a una especie sin nombrar con un hocico acortado, en cambio el espécimen de Ceratosaurus tenía un cráneo alto, ancho y corto, con dientes con forma curvada, con un hocico largo y los dientes inferiores verticales más largos.

facts.statement: In 1884, Marsh considered the nasal horn of Ceratosaurus a powerful offensive and defensive weapon, a view agreed upon by Gilmore in 1920.
facts.quote: Marsh en un estudio en el año de 1884 consideró que el cuerno nasal de Ceratosaurus pudo ser un "arma poderosa" a las reacciones tanto ofensivas como defensivas, y Gilmore en 1920 está de acuerdo con este análisis.

facts.statement: However, the idea that the nasal horn was a powerful weapon is generally considered unlikely.
facts.quote: Sin embargo, esta interpretación es considerada generalmente poco probable.

facts.statement: In 1985, Norman suggested the horn was likely not for defense against predators but for intraspecific combat, possibly by males fighting for mating rights.
facts.quote: Norman en 1985 creyó que el cuerno era "probablemente no para la protección contra otros depredadores", pero podría en cambio haberse utilizado para el combate intraespecífico, pero mencionó que es más posible que los machos hayan luchado con este cuerno, por los derechos de apareamiento.

facts.statement: In 1988, Paul suggested the nasal horn had another function, illustrated by two Ceratosaurus engaging in a non-lethal head-butting duel.
facts.quote: Paul en el año de 1988 sugirió que el cuerno nasal de Ceratosaurus tenía otra función, ilustrado a dos Ceratosaurus participando en un duelo de cabezazos, no letal.

facts.statement: In 1990, Rowe and Gauthier suggested the nasal horn was likely used only for display and played no role in physical confrontations.
facts.quote: Rowe y Gauthier en 1990 fueron más allá, sugiriendo que el cuerno nasal de Ceratosaurus fue "probablemente utilizado para fines de visualización solamente" y no desempeñaron ningún papel en confrontaciones físicas.

facts.statement: If the nasal horn was used for display, it is probable that the horn would have been brightly colored.
facts.quote: Si el cuerno nasal de Ceratosaurus se utilizaba para la visualización, es probable que el cuerno habría sido de colores brillantes.

facts.statement: In 2001, Bruce Rothschild and others published an examination of stress fracture evidence in theropod dinosaurs.
facts.quote: En el 2001, Bruce Rothschild y otros publicaron un examen de la evidencia del estudio de las fracturas por estrés en dinosaurios terópodos.

facts.statement: They examined a single foot bone of the Ceratosaurus nasicornis holotype and found it had a stress fracture.
facts.quote: Ellos examinaron un solo hueso del pie del Holotipo de Ceratosaurus nasicornis y encontraron que tenía una fractura por estrés.

facts.statement: In the Ceratosaurus nasicornis holotype USMN 4735, the left metatarsals 2 through 4 were found to be fused.
facts.quote: En el espécimen Holotipo de Ceratosaurus nasicornis, USMN 4735, se encontró que sus metatarsianos 2 a 4 izquierdos estaban fusionados.

facts.statement: An unnamed species of Ceratosaurus preserves a broken tooth showing signs of wear received after eating.
facts.quote: Una especie no nombrada de Ceratosaurus conserva un diente roto que muestra señales de desgaste recibido después de haber comido.

facts.statement: The parent group of Ceratosaurus is Ceratosauria.
facts.quote: Parent group: Ceratosauria

facts.statement: Ceratosaurus is classified in the class Reptilia.
facts.quote: Class: Reptilia

facts.statement: If C. ingens is valid, at least one species of Ceratosaurus was as large as Torvosaurus and Epanterias that lived alongside it.
facts.quote: Si C. ingens es válido, por lo menos una especie de Ceratosaurus era tan grande como Torvosaurus y Epanterias que vivieron junto a este.

facts.statement: It is debated whether C. ingens is a carcarodontosaurid and whether C. stechowi is a ceratosaurian or a spinosaurid.
facts.quote: Pero ahora cree que posiblemente C. ingens es un carcarodontosáurido, y que C. stechowi es un ceratosauriano o un espinosáurido.

facts.statement: A 2026 study argues that the dentition of Ceratosaurus might have been an adaptation for quickly killing middle-sized prey.
facts.quote: Oswald & Curtice (2026) report evidence of similarities between the morphometrics of teeth of Ceratosaurus and upper canines of machairodontines, and argue that the dentition of the former might have been an adaptation to quick-killing middle-sized prey.

facts.statement: A 2026 study reported evidence that Ceratosaurus skull adaptations suggest similarities in ecological roles with abelisaurs and tyrannosaurs.
facts.quote: Rowe, Cerroni & Rayfield (2026) study mechanical performance of skulls of Ceratosaurus, Masiakasaurus, Carnotaurus and Majungasaurus, and report evidence of adaptations of skulls of large abelisaurs to resist feeding-induced loads, suggestive of similarity of ecological roles of abelisaurs and tyrannosaurs, as well as possible evidence of adaptation of Masiakasaurus to capture of small prey.
